title: The Namesake
author: Jhumpa Lahiri
citation: Lahiri, Jhumpa. The Namesake. Houghton Mifflin, 2003.

sections.heading: The Namesake (Chapters 1, 2, 5, 8, and 12 Key Selections)

epigraph.quote: The man who gave you his name from the book that gave you your father.

paragraphs: Ashima Ganguli stands in the kitchen of a Central Square apartment in Cambridge, Massachusetts, combining Rice Krispies and Planters peanuts and chopped red onion in a bowl. It is 1968. She is nine months pregnant, and she is trying to recreate the spicy street food called jhalmuri that she used to buy from vendors on the sidewalks of Calcutta. But nothing tastes right; the spices of New England cannot replace the memories of Bengal.

When her son is born in Mount Auburn Hospital, he has no official name. In Bengali tradition, every person has two names: a daknam, or pet name, used only by family and intimate friends, and a bhalonam, a formal 'good name' used on legal documents and in school. Ashima and her husband Ashoke are waiting for a letter from Ashima's grandmother in Calcutta, who has been given the honor of selecting the boy's formal name. But the letter never arrives, lost somewhere in the mail between India and America.

In the hospital, the registrar insists that a name must be recorded on the birth certificate before the baby can be discharged. Desperate, Ashoke remembers the miracle that saved his life. Years earlier, in 1961, as a college student traveling by night train from Calcutta to Jamshedpur, Ashoke had been reading a volume of Nikolai Gogol's short stories. At three in the morning, the train derailed in a catastrophic crash, telescoping the passenger cars into mangled steel. Ashoke lay pinned in the wreckage, paralyzed, clutching a single page of Gogol's 'The Overcoat.' When searchers shone their flashlights through the debris, they saw the flutter of the book page in his bloody fingers and pulled him out alive.

Looking down at his newborn son in the glass bassinet, Ashoke whispers: 'Gogol.' The baby is named for the Russian author whose book had saved his father from the grave. For the first fourteen years of his life, Gogol Ganguli accepts his pet name without question. He grows up in suburban Boston, eats samosas and pot roasts, attends Bengali pujas and American Little League games, comfortable in his two worlds.

But as adolescence arrives, Gogol begins to hate his name. It is neither Indian nor American. It belongs to an eccentric, melancholy Russian writer who starved himself to death. Girls giggle when they hear it; teachers stumble over it on the first day of class. On his eighteenth birthday, his father presents him with a hardbound volume of Gogol's collected stories, inscribed: 'The man who gave you his name from the book that gave you your father.' But the adolescent Gogol cannot grasp the depth of his father's gratitude; he stuffs the book into the bottom of his closet.

Before leaving for college at Yale, he goes to court and legally changes his name to Nikhil. As Nikhil, he reinvents himself: he dates white American girls, studies architecture, rents an apartment in Manhattan, and distances himself from his parents' Bengali enclave in Massachusetts. Yet no matter how hard he tries to bury Gogol, the ghost of his original name follows him like a shadow.

Only after his father dies suddenly of a heart attack in an Ohio hospital does Nikhil begin to understand the gift he had rejected. Sitting alone in his childhood bedroom on Christmas Eve, with the family home about to be sold, he discovers the long-forgotten volume of Gogol's stories tucked behind old textbooks. He opens the yellowed cover, traces his father's handwriting, and begins to read 'The Overcoat' for the very first time.
